description: Pipeline plugin hooks. Every command routes through `hooks/run-hook.sh`, which resolves an absolute `pipeline` binary (PATH → $BUN_INSTALL/bin → ~/.bun/bin → /opt/homebrew/bin → /usr/local/bin) and runs `pipeline hook <name>` with stdin/stdout/stderr inherited — Claude Code runs hooks through a non-interactive /bin/sh that never sources ~/.zshrc, so a Dock- or Start-menu-launched session cannot otherwise see a global install. EVERY COMMAND HOOK BELOW PINS THE SHELL: `"shell": "bash"` sits beside `"type"` and `"command"` on all TEN of them (Stop 2, SubagentStop 2, SessionStart 2, PreToolUse 1, PostToolUse 1, UserPromptSubmit 1, Notification 1), and the pin is load-bearing rather than cosmetic (T-CLI-2 remedy, ROADMAP row B.5). Omitted, Claude Code picks Git Bash on Windows and FALLS BACK TO POWERSHELL when Git Bash is not installed — which hands this POSIX-sh shim to a shell that cannot execute it. That fallback was measured (T-CLI-2 / v1, PR #122) as either a hang or, worse, a dispatcher that exits 0 WITHOUT running the shim at all, which on PreToolUse turns a deny-hook into a permit: a security control that FAILS OPEN. Pinning to `bash` makes Git Bash a hard Windows prerequisite — Git for Windows (https://git-scm.com/download/win) bundles it, or `winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget`, and README's Install section states this as the third prerequisite. Without it the hooks FAIL VISIBLY instead of silently doing nothing, and that is the intended trade — but visibility is ALL it buys, and THE PIN DOES NOT MAKE THE CONTROL FAIL CLOSED. Verified against the installed Claude Code dispatcher: a bash-pinned hook on a Windows machine with no detected Git Bash throws BEFORE the spawn, outside the spawn's own try, and the hook runner classifies that as outcome `non_blocking_error` (surfaced as `hook_non_blocking_error`, deduped per event+command per session, so about ten messages and then silence). THE TOOL CALL STILL PROCEEDS. The only path that yields outcome `blocking` is a hook that actually RAN and exited 2. So a bash-pinned PreToolUse deny-hook on a Git-Bash-less Windows box still reads as an ALLOW — an announced one, rather than one indistinguishable from a hook that ran and approved. Do not build a genuinely blocking PreToolUse hook on top of this file expecting the platform to hold it closed; it will not. macOS and Linux are unaffected. Add a new command hook and it must carry the pin too — miss one and that single event keeps the fail-open path while every other event looks fixed. A PowerShell twin of `run-hook.sh` was considered and REJECTED by the owner (2026-08-19): a second shim is a permanent drift surface, and one shell plus an honest prerequisite is the cheaper contract. The shim also absorbs VERSION SKEW: a CLI too old to know the `hook` subcommand refuses it with exit 2, which on PreToolUse would block the tool call, so the shim classifies a non-zero exit with a read-only `pipeline hook --help` probe and exits 0 (one actionable upgrade line under --loud) only when the subcommand is genuinely absent; a relay that ran and failed still propagates its exit code. THE RELAYS ARE CLI SUBCOMMANDS, NOT FILES IN THIS PLUGIN (plugin-thin p6): they live in `IvanMurzak/pipeline` as `src/hooks/*.ts`, so a hook's version is the installed CLI's version by construction. This plugin therefore REQUIRES `@baizor/pipeline` — `bun add -g @baizor/pipeline` — and the --loud SessionStart entry below is what says so when it is missing. Registrations: Stop → analytics relay (token usage from transcript) then stats relay (token + tool-failure enrichment for .pipeline/.stats/); SubagentStop (matcher: pipeline-manager) → analytics relay (manager.stopped liveness signal when a pipeline-manager subagent ends — the matcher keeps the hook from spawning for every other subagent) then stats relay; Notification → analytics relay (run.awaiting_input when a permission prompt or an input request blocks the session); SessionStart → the session relay (appends one session.opened line to the project's .runtime/events.jsonl and nothing else — this is what is left of the deleted local dashboard's launcher hook, kept because the journal is ux-v2's telemetry source and `pipeline logs` renders the event), THEN the department notifier relay (department-mesh task a1: ensures the `pipeline department notify` background daemon is running detached and drains its pending-notification journal into SessionStart additionalContext — a department task that reaches INPUT_REQUIRED/AUTH_REQUIRED or a terminal state announces itself even across sessions, gated by its own switch PIPELINE_DEPARTMENT_NOTIFY_ENABLED (falling back to the deprecated PIPELINE_MESH_NOTIFY_ENABLED with a warning), default ON, no-op until `pipeline cloud connect` has been run once); PreToolUse → analytics relay (live mirror binding + run-level bypass START synthesis for pipeline-manager spawns); PostToolUse → analytics relay (tool counts + agent spawns + bypass END/fallback lifecycle synthesis); UserPromptSubmit → prompt match relay (BM25-matches the submitted prompt against the project's PIPELINE.md manifests and, on a confident single match only, injects one line of additionalContext suggesting the pipeline — gated by its own opt-in switch PIPELINE_PROMPT_MATCH_ENABLED, off by default). The whole journal/analytics system is ON BY DEFAULT — every journal hook runs at entry unless PIPELINE_JOURNAL_ENABLED is explicitly opted out with a falsy value 0/false/no/off (the master opt-OUT switch; the prompt match relay is a separate OPT-IN gated by PIPELINE_PROMPT_MATCH_ENABLED instead, off by default) — and is additionally a no-op when cwd has no .pipeline/ (the department notifier relay is independent of this project-scoped gate — department tasks are org-scoped, not project-scoped, so it runs the same in every directory, gated only by PIPELINE_DEPARTMENT_NOTIFY_ENABLED). EXCEPTION: Stop and SubagentStop additionally run the stats relay (token + tool-failure enrichment for the per-run measurement files under .pipeline/.stats/, via the shared backfillProject core), which is ON BY DEFAULT and gated by its own PIPELINE_STATS_ENABLED (set 0 to disable); it too no-ops when the project has no .stats dir. SECOND EXCEPTION: the Notification branch is evaluated BEFORE the PIPELINE_JOURNAL_ENABLED opt-out and carries its own gate PIPELINE_AWAITING_INPUT_ENABLED (default ON, set 0 to disable) — a blocked run is worth surfacing through `pipeline logs` even for a user who is not connected to the cloud dashboard. PER-HOOK TIMEOUTS: every command hook below carries an explicit `timeout`, in SECONDS, sitting beside `type`/`command`/`shell`. Until now none did, so every hook inherited Claude Code's default — 600s (TEN MINUTES) on every event registered here except `UserPromptSubmit`, which defaults to 30s. `run-hook.sh` names this exact lever in its own comments ("the lever is `hooks.json`'s per-hook `timeout` field, not shell code here"), and this is it. WHAT A TIMEOUT ACTUALLY DOES HERE IS NARROWER THAN IT SOUNDS, AND THE DISTINCTION IS LOAD-BEARING — IT IS ALSO NOT THE SAME FOR AN EXPLICIT `timeout` AS FOR THE DEFAULT CAP, WHICH IS THE TRAP. Under the DEFAULT cap, expiry is abandonment: `run-hook.sh` measured a hook sleeping 70s under a 30s default cap as cancelled (`timedOut: true`, `timeoutMs: 30000`) with its `durationMs` still reading 70619 — the process ran all 70 seconds. AN EXPLICITLY-CONFIGURED `timeout`, WHICH IS WHAT THIS FILE NOW SHIPS, DOES NOT BEHAVE THAT WAY: measured directly against Claude Code 2.1.237 with a `"timeout": 5` on a hook that heartbeats every 500ms, the hook process was KILLED 5,375ms into its own run and its post-sleep marker was never written, while the session went on for another 3.5s — so the cap terminated it rather than merely stopping the wait. DO NOT GENERALISE THE `run-hook.sh` MEASUREMENT ONTO THIS FIELD; they are different mechanisms and only one of them was ever measured here before. THE RELAYS SURVIVE IT ANYWAY, FOR A STRUCTURAL REASON WORTH KNOWING: the `hook` shape deliberately SPAWNS rather than `exec`s (see run-hook.sh's own comment on that choice), so the CLI is a GRANDCHILD of Claude Code, and in the same probe — same 5s cap, wrapper reproducing that spawn-not-exec shape — the wrapper was killed with its end-marker unwritten while THE GRANDCHILD RAN TO COMPLETION, all forty heartbeats across 39 seconds, writing its own end marker long after the shim was gone. So for these ten hooks the turn is released, the hook's output is DISCARDED (a cancelled hook's stderr appeared zero times in the transcript), and the relay finishes its work in the background uninterrupted. That last part is a property of the spawn-not-exec shape, NOT of the timeout — a hook that `exec`ed the relay, or did the work in the shim itself, WOULD be cut off mid-write. Anyone flattening that spawn into an `exec` for tidiness would silently take on exactly the mid-write exposure this file otherwise does not have. A `PreToolUse` timeout does not block the tool either. Hooks for one event run in parallel, each with its own timeout. THE VALUES ARE MEASURED end-to-end through this shim, with every invocation's exit code and stderr asserted so a silently-failing measurement cannot masquerade as a fast one — the first attempt at this measurement made exactly that mistake, sending payloads whose Windows paths were invalid JSON, so every stdin-reading relay bailed at the parse and produced uniformly fast, uniformly meaningless numbers. NINE OF THE TEN ENTRIES GET 20s. On a Windows 11 box against a 63MB transcript the hot path — `PostToolUse` → analytics — costs 291ms on its own, 1.24s with eight hooks running at once and 4.49s with thirty-two, so 20s is about 4.4× the worst contended case and a machine several times slower is still never cut off. Transcript SIZE barely matters to analytics (2KB, 16MB and 64MB all land between 150ms and 550ms) because it tails from a stored byte offset rather than re-reading, and `prompt-match` is likewise flat — 200 pipeline manifests cost no more than one. The department notifier is NOT the slow relay its description might suggest: its daemon spawn is DETACHED, so ensuring the daemon runs costs what skipping it costs (354-1149ms either way). THE ONE OUTLIER IS `SubagentStop` → stats-relay, AT 60s, and the reason is measured scaling and nothing else. It is the single path the CLI's own source declares UNBUDGETED — its `Stop` sibling self-bounds at STOP_BUDGET_MS = 4000 and measures under 1.6s even with fifty stale records, which is why that sibling sits on the floor at 20s. This one's cost scales with STALE RECORDS × TRANSCRIPT BYTES, not with either alone: against a 63MB transcript it took 0.9s with no `tokens: null` records to reconcile, 1.8s with five, 4.6s with twenty and 9.1s with fifty — and 11.1s for the twenty-record case once eight hooks were competing for the box. A `.stats` tree carrying a backlog while a larger transcript is in play extrapolates past 45s, so this entry is not put on the floor. Cancelling any of the ten is safe: they are best-effort telemetry, an abandoned fold simply leaves the record null for a later stop to fill, and not one of them is a blocking control. `UserPromptSubmit` is the one entry whose cap was LOWERED rather than introduced — it already defaulted to 30s, it holds the user's prompt for as long as it runs, and it measured well under 1s even with 200 manifests, so 20s tightens it and still leaves ample headroom. Add a new command hook and it MUST carry a timeout too: `tests/hook-run-shim.test.ts` pins THESE EXACT VALUES — nine entries at 20s and `SubagentStop` → stats-relay at 60s, named individually — as well as the 5-60s range, so this paragraph and the file cannot drift apart without CI saying so. Retuning a value is therefore a deliberate two-file edit, which is the point.
